# Simulated example {#sec-quickstart}

```{r}
#| label: sim-setup
library(sconjoint)
house <- "#004a8c"
truth <- simconjoint_truth$population
tv <- function(name) truth$value[truth$name == name]
t_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
```

The package's `simconjoint` data hold 800 simulated respondents who each choose between two
candidates ten times. Their tastes are known. For example,
`r round(100 * tv("share: prefer Republican"), 1)`% of the population prefers a Republican
candidate to an otherwise identical Democrat, and long experience raises a candidate's chance of
being chosen by `r round(100 * tv("AME: long vs no experience"), 1)` percentage points on average.
This chapter runs the whole workflow on these data and compares the estimates with the truth.

The chapter runs live, in about five minutes on a recent laptop. It uses a small network and
modest integration rules. The paper's larger settings would give somewhat tighter answers.

## Experiment

Each candidate has four attributes, each drawn at random and independently: party, experience,
policy position and gender. The data hold one row per candidate, two rows per task.

```{r}
#| label: sim-data
head(simconjoint, 4)
```

Each respondent has three characteristics: age, ideology on a seven-point scale from $-3$ (very
liberal) to 3 (very conservative), and gender.

`sc_design()` describes how the candidates were drawn and codes each attribute as one 0/1
indicator per level other than the first, six coded features in all. `sc_code()` turns the two
candidates of each task into their difference, first minus second.

```{r}
#| label: sim-design
des <- sc_design(list(party = c("Democrat", "Republican"),
                      experience = c("none", "some", "long"),
                      position = c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"),
                      gender = c("male", "female")), tasks = 10)
des
A <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 1, ]          # first (left) candidate of each task
B <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 2, ]
X <- sc_code(des, A, B)
head(X, 3)
```

`sc_data()` collects the choices (1 when the first candidate was chosen), the coded differences,
the respondent ids, and the characteristics that predict mean tastes. With the design attached,
`sc_states()` later averages over the comparisons each respondent could have seen.

```{r}
#| label: sim-scdata
Z <- as.matrix(A[!duplicated(A$id), c("age", "ideology", "female")])
rownames(Z) <- unique(A$id)
x <- sc_data(A$chosen, X, A$id, Z = Z, groups = data.frame(female = Z[, "female"]), design = des,
             orientation = "y = 1 selects the first (left) candidate; X = first minus second")
x
```

## Truth

The choices follow the package's model (@sec-intro): tastes $\beta_i = \mu(Z_i) + \Lambda u_i$
with two taste factors, and a pull $a_i = \sqrt{\omega}\, v_i$ toward the left candidate on top of
the average pull $\kappa$. Here $\kappa = 0.2$ and $\omega = 0.3$. The taste for a Republican
rises with ideology and flattens out for strong partisans. Older respondents value experience
more. Policy tastes follow a loss around the respondent's own position. The first taste factor
moves party and policy, the second experience and gender. `?simconjoint` gives every formula.

```{r}
#| label: sim-truth
simconjoint_truth$parameters[c("kappa", "omega")]
simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading
```

`simconjoint_truth$population` holds the population values, exact sums over the finite set of
characteristic values with inner integrals computed by quadrature to about $10^{-6}$ or better.

## Fits

`sc_fit()` fits the model once per fold, each time on the other four of five folds. The code fits
one, two and three taste factors with one hidden layer of 8 units, one start, at most 100 epochs,
and Sobol rules of 128 to 256 nodes.

```{r}
#| label: sim-fit
small <- list(hidden = 8L, seeds = 1L, control = list(max_epochs = 100L, patience = 5L),
              nodes = 128L, check_nodes = 256L, heldout_nodes = 256L, verbose = FALSE)
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fits <- lapply(1:3, function(q) do.call(sc_fit, c(list(x, q = q), small)))
t_fit <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

## Number of factors

`sc_select_rank()` scores each fit on the respondents it did not train on. It moves from $q - 1$
to $q$ factors only when the held-out log score gains more than two standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank
rank <- sc_select_rank(fits)
rank
fit <- fits[[which(rank$selected)]]
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank-text
#| echo: false
q_sel <- rank$q[rank$selected]
```

The rule picks $q = `r q_sel`$`r if (q_sel == 2) ", the true number" else ", not the true number, 2"`. The second
factor improves the held-out score by `r round(rank$z[2], 1)` standard errors. The third changes it
by `r round(rank$z[3], 1)`, which is noise. Two factors are needed because respondents with the
same characteristics still differ in two ways: how strongly partisan they are, and how much they
care about experience and gender.

## Fold states

`sc_states()` computes what the estimator needs from each fold's fit. The slow part is each
held-out respondent's information, an average over task sets drawn from `des`, which `x` carries.
The code uses 40 draws per respondent, the paper 250 to 300.

```{r}
#| label: sim-states
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
st <- sc_states(fit, M = 40L, ny = 4L, info_nodes = 256L, score_nodes = 512L)
t_states <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
st
```

## Estimates

Each target names one population quantity (@sec-quantities). The compensating share is the share
for whom party outweighs experience: they would take a Republican with no experience over a
Democrat with long experience. The contest compares a moderate Republican woman with long
experience to a liberal Democrat man with some experience, with position effects set to zero.
`sc_ame_switch()` and `sc_importance(des)` take their contexts and attributes from the design.

```{r}
#| label: sim-estimate
contest <- sc_code(des, data.frame(party = "Republican", experience = "long", position = "moderate", gender = "female"),
                   data.frame(party = "Democrat", experience = "some", position = "liberal", gender = "male"))
targets <- list(
  sc_mean("mean: Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_mean("mean: long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_mean("mean: conservative position", "position_conservative"),
  sc_mean("mean: female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: prefer Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_share("share: prefer long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_share("share: prefer female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: Republican without experience over Democrat with long",
           c(party_Republican = 1, experience_long = -1)),
  sc_contest("contest: A beats B", drop(contest)),
  sc_ame_switch("AME: long vs no experience", "experience", level = "long", ref = "none"),
  sc_importance(des, names = paste("importance:", names(des$attributes))))
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
est <- sc_estimate(st, targets)
t_est <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
est$truth <- truth$value[match(est$name, truth$name)]
est$covered <- est$truth >= est$lower & est$truth <= est$upper
knitr::kable(est[, c("name", "truth", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "covered")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Quantity", "Truth", "Estimate", "95% lower", "95% upper", "Covered"))
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-cover
#| echo: false
n_int <- sum(!is.na(est$covered)); n_cov <- sum(est$covered, na.rm = TRUE)
miss <- est$name[which(!est$covered)]
imp <- which(est$kind == "importance"); imp_worst <- imp[which.max(abs(est$estimate[imp] - est$truth[imp]))]
imp_err <- abs(est$estimate[imp_worst] - est$truth[imp_worst])
resp <- simconjoint_truth$respondents; law <- simconjoint_truth$covariate_law
cons_sample <- mean(resp$ideology > 0); cons_pop <- sum(law$ideology_probs[law$ideology > 0])
party_sample <- mean(simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"])
r_party <- est[est$name == "mean: Republican", ]
```

`r n_cov` of the `r n_int` intervals cover the truth`r if (length(miss)) paste0("; the miss", if (length(miss) > 1) "es are " else " is ", paste0("\"", miss, "\"", collapse = ", ")) else ""`.
With 95% intervals, about one miss in twenty is expected, so one run cannot show that coverage
is exact. The intervals are for the population, and this sample of 800 leans right. It holds more
conservatives than the population (`r round(100 * cons_sample)`% against
`r round(100 * cons_pop)`%), and its true average taste for a Republican is
`r round(party_sample, 2)`, against `r round(r_party$truth, 2)` in the population. The interval for
that mean, from `r round(r_party$lower, 2)` to `r round(r_party$upper, 2)`,
`r if (isTRUE(r_party$covered)) "covers the population value" else "covers the sample's value but not the population's"`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-estimates
#| fig-cap: "Estimates and 95% intervals (blue) against the truth (open circles)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
short <- c("Republican", "Long experience", "Conservative position", "Female candidate",
           "Prefer Republican", "Prefer long experience", "Prefer female candidate",
           "Rep., no exp., over Dem., long exp.", "Contest: A beats B", "AME: long experience",
           paste("Importance:", names(des$attributes)))
lab <- setNames(short, est$name)
truth_of <- setNames(est$truth, est$name)
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(1, 1.3), heights = c(4, .45))
sc_plot_estimates(est[1:4, ], labels = lab, reference = truth_of, reference_style = "circle",
                  xlim = c(-.3, .9), xlab = "Mean taste (logit scale)", legend = FALSE)
sc_plot_estimates(est[5:14, ], labels = lab, reference = truth_of, reference_style = "circle",
                  xlim = c(0, .85), xlab = "Share or probability", legend = FALSE)
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
keys <- c("Estimate and 95% interval", "Truth", "No interval")
legend("center", keys, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", pch = c(16, 1, 1), lty = c(1, NA, NA),
       col = c(house, "black", house), pt.cex = c(.8, 1.2, .8), cex = .85,
       text.width = strwidth(paste0(keys, "mm"), cex = .85))
```

The left panel shows mean tastes, the right panel shares, probabilities, the AME and importance
shares. Importance shares have no intervals. In this run their largest miss is `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points, for
`r sub("importance: ", "", est$name[imp_worst])`, so read them as rough.

Two population mean tastes, for party and policy, are close to zero. That does not mean
respondents do not care (@fig-sim-laws).

## Taste distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` gives each held-out respondent's fitted normal law of a taste, with mean
$c^\top\mu(Z_i)$ and standard deviation $\lVert\Lambda^\top c\rVert$. Their mixture is the fitted
distribution. The true one uses the true $\mu$ and $\Lambda$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-laws
#| fig-cap: "Fitted (blue) and true (black) distributions of two tastes"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
L0 <- simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading; mu0 <- simconjoint_truth$mu
sf <- c("party_Republican", "experience_long")
true_law <- function(f) function(v)          # the true density: a mixture over respondents
  rowMeans(outer(v, mu0[, f], function(g, m) dnorm(g, m, sqrt(sum(L0[f, ]^2)))))
sc_plot_laws(lapply(sf, function(f) sc_fitted_law(st, f)),
             labels = c("Taste for a Republican", "Taste for long experience"),
             truth = lapply(sf, true_law), layout = "panels", ncol = 2, xlim = c(-3.5, 3.5),
             xlab = "Taste (logit scale)")
```

The true taste for a Republican has two humps, liberals below zero and conservatives above. The
fitted distribution has the right width, from about $-3$ to $3$, but blurs the humps into a
plateau. The 8-unit network learns a mean taste almost linear in ideology, while the truth,
$2 \tanh(3s)$ with $s$ the ideology divided by 3, levels off away from the centre. The fit makes
up for this with a larger spread (the table below). A network with two hidden layers (16 and 8
units) found the humps in our trials but predicted held-out choices worse, so the held-out score
prefers the smoother fit. The shares and means are
still right, because they depend only on the mass above zero and the centre. The taste for long
experience has one hump, recovered almost exactly, about three quarters of it above zero.

The loading $\Lambda$ itself is not identified: any rotation of its columns gives the same model.
The spread of tastes among respondents with the same characteristics, $\Lambda\Lambda^\top$, is
identified. Its diagonal gives each taste's standard deviation among such respondents. Averaged
over the five folds:

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread
sd_fit <- rowMeans(sapply(st$folds, function(f) sqrt(rowSums(as.matrix(f$th$loading)^2))))
spread <- data.frame(feature = des$features, true_sd = round(sqrt(rowSums(L0^2)), 2),
                     fitted_sd = round(sd_fit, 2), row.names = NULL)
spread
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread-text
#| echo: false
gap <- abs(spread$fitted_sd - spread$true_sd); j <- which.max(gap)
```

The fitted spread is within `r round(max(gap[-j]), 2)` of the truth for five of the six features.
The exception is `r spread$feature[j]` (`r spread$fitted_sd[j]` against `r spread$true_sd[j]`),
where the spread absorbs the part of the mean taste the network did not learn.

## Individual respondents

`sc_posterior()` combines the fitted law with a respondent's own choices, at the fold that did not
train on that respondent (@sec-respondents). `history` sets how many of the first tasks to use.

```{r}
#| label: sim-posterior
b_true <- simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"]
post <- lapply(c(0, 2, 5, 10), function(h)
  sc_posterior(st, contrasts = c(party_Republican = 1), history = h, nodes = 1024)$contrasts)
data.frame(tasks_used = c(0, 2, 5, 10),
           correlation = round(sapply(post, function(p) cor(p$mean, b_true)), 3),
           rmse = round(sapply(post, function(p) sqrt(mean((p$mean - b_true)^2))), 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean against true taste for a Republican"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (j in c(1, 4))
  sc_plot_posterior(post[[j]], truth = b_true, xlab = "True taste for a Republican",
                    main = c("No tasks used", "", "", "All 10 tasks")[j])
par(op)
```

With no tasks, the posterior mean is the fitted $\mu(Z_i)$, which already tracks the true taste
because ideology explains much of party taste. With all ten tasks, the correlation rises from `r round(cor(post[[1]]$mean, b_true), 2)`
to `r round(cor(post[[4]]$mean, b_true), 2)`. The points still scatter widely: ten choices
carry limited information, and the posterior pulls each respondent toward $\mu(Z_i)$. The
posterior is therefore a prediction of a respondent's taste, not a measurement of it. For
population questions, such as how many prefer a Republican, use the population targets above
rather than counts of posterior means.

## What is recovered

- **Recovered:** the number of taste factors; mean tastes, shares, the compensating share, the
  contest probability and the AME, with `r n_cov` of `r n_int` intervals covering the population
  value; the distribution of the taste for experience; the spread of most tastes; the position
  effects $\kappa$ and $\omega$ (each fold's values are in `summary(fit)`).
- **Recovered roughly:** importance shares, which have no intervals and miss here by up to
  `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points; the distribution of the taste for a Republican, with the
  right width but its two humps blurred into a plateau.
- **Not recovered:** the loading $\Lambda$ itself, identified only up to rotation; individual
  tastes, which ten tasks pin down only partly.

```{r}
#| label: sim-time
#| echo: false
t_total <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_start
```

This chapter took `r round(t_total / 60, 1)` minutes to run: `r round(t_fit / 60, 1)` for the
three fits, `r round(t_states / 60, 1)` for the fold states and `r round(t_est / 60, 1)` for the
estimates.

## Next steps

@sec-gs and @sec-br apply the same steps to the paper's data, starting from saved fits.
@sec-quantities lists every target. For another experiment with independently drawn attributes,
describe it with `sc_design()` and code its profiles with `sc_code()`. Every step above then works
unchanged.
